frameworks.name: Education-First Capital Allocation
frameworks.definition: A multi-year strategy of investing all available capital into skill-building education until earnings exceed reinvestment capacity, treating each purchased skill as time-value acceleration into future earning potential.

frameworks.name: Earning Power Compounding Loop
frameworks.definition: A recursive cycle where invested education increases annual income, excess income funds the next skill tier, and the process repeats until annual learning spend reaches zero percent of income.

claims.text: Investing in personal skill development consistently outperforms stock market returns (S&P 500 ~10% annually) because a person earning $50,000 can triple earning capacity to $150,000 in one year through targeted education, generating $100,000 in additional income versus the $900 return from $10,000 invested in equities.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Person willing to follow instructions and execute on learning
Education is in a high-leverage skill with direct income application
Baseline earning power is below $150k/year
claims.mechanism: Education directly multiplies earning capacity; stock returns are linear additions whereas skill multipliers are exponential on the income base.
bounded_by: Assumes person has no specialized skills to begin with
Assumes education is high-quality and applicable to income-generating work
Does not apply once person is in top income bracket where further earning increases are marginal

claims.text: The hidden annual cost of not possessing a million-dollar earning skill is the difference between current earnings and what could be earned — a person making $50,000 effectively pays reality $950,000 per year for lacking the skill to make $1M, even though they don't write a check for it.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Person has capacity to acquire the skill
Market opportunity exists for million-dollar earning power
Skill acquisition is within realistic timeframe
claims.mechanism: Opportunity cost frames the annual economic loss from skill gap; the gap itself represents invisible wealth transfer.

numbers.axis: annual opportunity cost of skill gap

bounded_by: Does not apply when person has limited capacity to execute the skill

claims.text: Spending all accumulated capital on skill-building education is justified because each dollar of education spend maps to multiples of future earning power, and the compounding effect of repeated skill acquisition compounds faster than market returns.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Person is below their earning ceiling
Education is selected for direct income leverage
Person will execute on what is learned
claims.mechanism: Each skill tier compounds earnings; reinvesting new earnings into the next skill tier accelerates the journey to the income level where education spend becomes optional.
bounded_by: Does not apply once earnings exceed $1M+ annually where further optimization yields diminishing returns
Does not apply to speculative or unproven education programs

claims.text: Paying for education from practitioners in active businesses (who live in 'real private businesses' running actual operations) is superior to paying academics who have not been in market reality for 20 years, because practitioners have incentive alignment with student outcomes.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Education cost is significant ($2k-$30k per program)
Student intends to apply knowledge to income-generating work
Practitioner has ongoing business generating revenue
claims.mechanism: Practitioners depend on student success for reputation and referrals, creating outcome-based incentive; academics on tenure have no market feedback mechanism.
bounded_by: Does not apply to purely theoretical education where practitioner experience is not relevant
Does not apply when academic institution provides credentialing necessary for the target industry

claims.text: A student's outcome is jointly determined by program quality AND student commitment; a student choosing to apply program teachings despite sub-optimal program quality will outperform a student dismissing the program while blaming its quality, making 'I will be your biggest success story' the load-bearing variable.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Program contains at least some actionable frameworks
Student has agency to execute independently if needed
claims.mechanism: Student agency and learning orientation determine outcome more than program optimization, because learning often comes from removing what doesn't work rather than accepting what is taught verbatim.
bounded_by: Does not apply if program is fraudulent or actively harmful
Does not apply if student lacks baseline capability to execute

claims.text: Buying education is buying the future at a discount; if personal skill development could take 5 years independently but 1 year with paid expert help across 4 steps, the full-cost education path is superior because it delivers 4 years of additional earning at the new baseline.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: buying the future at a discount
conditions: Person has capital available
Time value of accelerated earning is material relative to education cost
Expert guidance reduces time-to-competency by at least 50%
claims.mechanism: Time acceleration from guided learning compounds across all future earnings; living 4-5 years ahead financially (while chronologically younger) creates exponential wealth advantage.

numbers.axis: years of earnings acceleration per education investment

anchors.value: 1 year to target earning level + 4 years compounding at new baseline

bounded_by: Does not apply if expert guidance is ineffective or misaligned
Does not apply if time acceleration does not materially change opportunity access

claims.text: The question 'Will you pay $950,000 to make $1,000,000 and earn $1,000,000 every year thereafter?' is answered 'yes' by definition because a one-time skill cost with lifetime earnings benefit is a superior deal to any stock market return.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Skill is truly replicable and retains value over multiple years
Market opportunity for $1M earning level remains stable
claims.mechanism: Lifetime value of a skill vastly exceeds single-year cost because earnings are perpetual after one-time education spend.

claims.text: The progression from $1M to $10M annual earnings requires willing 100% of the $1M into education and infrastructure, because $1M earning power at saturation still has 9x growth potential available and the cost-to-acquire-that-growth is the 100% annual spend.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Person is earning stable $1M+/year
Market opportunity exists for 10x scaling
Person has team/systems to absorb new capabilities
claims.mechanism: At scale, available earning power (9x gap) vastly outweighs annual reinvestment cost, making 100% reinvestment a mathematically sound decision.

anchors.region: Education cost to achieve next tier

claims.text: Education spend of $200,000/year in $2,000-$5,000 and $30,000 chunks (conferences, seminars, coaching) is justified for a person earning $1M+/year because the 20% investment rate generates outsized skill compounding and preserves the optionality for the next 10x tier.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Person earning $1M+/year
Education is sourced from active practitioners
claims.mechanism: 20% education spend maintains skill velocity and prevents capability ceiling; marginal cost of next tier is lower when continuous learning is active.

numbers.axis: education spend as percentage of $1M annual income

claims.text: When a person achieves capability in an area (e.g., becomes best student in a program), the success is jointly attributable to program quality and student commitment; the person faces a choice between claiming the success (attributing it to self-effort) or dismissing the program (attributing it to luck), and this choice determines whether they compound success or stall.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Person has completed education program and achieved measurable results
Person has agency to continue or pivot
claims.mechanism: Claiming success via self-effort (and crediting program inputs) enables recursive application to next programs and domains; dismissing success blocks compounding because insight is rejected.

claims.text: Learning often comes from identifying what doesn't work (removal of bad practices) rather than from direct acceptance of what is taught; a person learning from bad instructors can extract as much value as learning from good instructors if they reverse-engineer the failures.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Person has framework to identify what's bad (empirical feedback)
Person can reverse-engineer the bad patterns into good ones
claims.mechanism: Identifying non-working patterns is equally valuable data as identifying working patterns because both narrow the solution space.
bounded_by: Does not apply when learning source is fraudulent or intentionally deceptive

claims.text: A person willing to spend time to become skilled (following instructions, showing up on time, failing and continuing) will receive positive ROI from virtually any education program because baseline discipline is the limiting factor, not program quality.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Education program contains at least some valid frameworks or skills
Person executes with discipline
Person applies learning to income-generating work
claims.mechanism: Execution discipline multiplies program quality; a disciplined student outperforms an undisciplined student in the same program by such a wide margin that program quality becomes secondary.
bounded_by: Does not apply to fraudulent programs designed to extract money
Does not apply when program contains actively harmful information

claims.text: The value of a skill is the economic difference between current earning capacity and earning capacity with the skill; people wildly undervalue this difference because they cannot see the counterfactual (earnings they are not making).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Skill is genuinely applicable to income generation
Market exists for the skill output
claims.mechanism: Invisible opportunity cost (earnings foregone) is psychologically unmemorable compared to visible costs (tuition paid), causing systematic undervaluation of skill value.

claims.text: Expertness is achieved by doing more repetitions than anyone else in a narrow field, which necessarily means failing more times than anyone else in that field; the person who wants to be an expert must accept that volume of failure is non-negotiable.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Field is chosen and commitment is made
Person has capital or time to sustain failures
claims.mechanism: Failure volume is the cost of repetition volume; mastery cannot be decoupled from failure density.

examples.text: A presenter writes $1,000,000 on a whiteboard in front of an audience, then asks a woman in the front row how much she makes. She answers $50,000. He then says: 'You pay reality $950,000 every year for not knowing how to make a million dollars.' This framing crystallizes opportunity cost from an invisible number ($950k foregone) into a visible comparison, and the woman immediately understands the value proposition of learning the skill.

Alex Hormozi spent capital almost every year on education programs ($2k-$30k chunks) during his scaling journey. Rather than wait for future earnings to arrive passively, he purchased the future at a discount by acquiring the skills required to compress the timeline. He progressed from earning $50k to $100k to $250k+ by reinvesting savings into education, then reinvesting new income into the next tier of education, until earnings were so high that education spend became immaterial. At each stage, he asked: 'Is there anything I could put this $50k into to 5-10x my earning power?' and consistently chose education over stock market investments.

When Alex Hormozi approaches an education program, he makes an explicit commitment: 'I will be your biggest success story.' This frames his relationship with the instructor as one where he takes responsibility for the outcome rather than blaming the program if he fails. He has applied this to every program, every partner, and every vendor he has worked with, and he reflects afterward on whether success was due to program quality or his own effort. This choice—claiming success and crediting the program—enables him to extract value from both excellent and mediocre instructors because he reverse-engineers what works and what doesn't.

practices.text: Ask yourself: 'Is there anything I could put this capital into that would 3-5x my earning capacity?' before investing passively in the stock market or other low-leverage vehicles.

When selecting education programs, prefer practitioners in active private businesses over academics on tenure, because practitioners have market feedback on the quality of their teaching and incentive alignment with student success.

Approach every education program with the mindset 'I will be the biggest success story,' taking full responsibility for learning regardless of program quality, and commit to reverse-engineering both what works and what doesn't.

Spend all available capital on skill-building education until the point where annual earnings exceed annual education spend, at which point education becomes a percentage of income (e.g., 20%) rather than consuming all capital.

When progressing to the next earning tier, allocate 100% of current annual earnings to education and capability building, because the gap to the next tier represents massive available upside relative to the reinvestment cost.
